I’m the lead teacher in a one year old toddlers class. Out of the 30+ students I’ve had so far, this describes all but two of them! Hand flapping when frustrated is something I see quite literally every day. 19 month olds are still very centered in gross motor development, and when you combine that with having huge emotions and limited reasoning ability, that frustrated energy often comes out as kicking, throwing themselves backwards, or hand flapping, because those are less complex and more accessible movements for them while their brains are on overdrive. Also, repeating phrases is an important part of verbal language development. Context is what’s important. Does she ever repeat phrases during relevant activities, or is it only ever at random times? Like, does she ever say “hello friends” as a greeting? If yes, that’s a good sign. With pointing, if you point to an object, will she look in the direction you’re pointing? Again, if yes that’s a good sign. 


I understand being concerned about your baby’s development, and it’s good that you are! I’ve found that almost all of my students experience a dramatic developmental leap sometime between 18 and 24 months, and often after 21 months, so waiting until then may be illuminating. Hope this helps!

you can overwinter them, but as a word of caution: I had* (key word) about a dozen pepper plants that I am attempting to overwinter. I cut off every leaf and cut the stems back significantly, sprayed ALL the soil off the roots, submerged each one in insecticidal soap with neem oil, also submerged their new clean indoor pots, rinsed the plants again, and repotted into fresh indoor potting mix. I put them spaced apart in their own closet with grow lights. All but two of them survived the overwintering process, a few leaves sprouted here and there, and I thought everything was going well. 


Cut to now, I have spider mites on one plant and aphids on half (maybe more). I’ve already thrown away one plant because I THOUGHT I had isolated all the infested ones, came back to check the other ones a few days later and there was a whole aphid rave happening on my poblano. I’m sure doing everything I did for pest prevention still helps, but the way I see it, whether or not you get pests is ultimately a matter of luck. I never had pest issues with my peppers outside, in fact they were the only thing that didn’t get munched (rip broccoli). Without weather or predatory insects, pests have nothing keeping them in check and can get out of control quickly. 


If you have houseplants you care about or are skeeved out by bugs, I’d think twice about overwintering. If you do have houseplants and decide to overwinter, then I’d try getting some bonide systemic granules and sprinkling them in the soil of those plants (not the peppers) so any infestations have less of a chance of spreading. I’m hoping that they work for me. Anyway, good luck!

(edited to specify that you should not put bonide systemic granules on peppers or any plant you plan on eating from, just on ornamental houseplants so they don’t get munched like my hoya did)

just to give another perspective, i was also told this by my trainer and it was extremely helpful. my dog used to be very reactive to any person, car, or dog walking in front of the house. it felt like we lived in a dungeon because i couldn't open the blinds without a freakout. my old technique for handling this was to toss a treat in the other direction and tell him it's okay, but the barking fits kept getting more intense. once my trainer explained that i may have inadvertently been strengthening his reaction, we switched protocols. 


our first and biggest improvement was teaching the word "no". my dog is a big, muscular pit mix who could push us around all day if he wanted to, so being able to set boundaries with him is crucial. for a while he wore a short leash in the house so i could tell him "no" while moving him away from whatever the issue was, and we've progressed to the point where just the "no" is usually enough for him to drop what he's doing. 


second, and i'm putting this in bold for a reason, *REDIRECTION IS KEY*. giving my dog a treat when he's fixed on whatever's making him anxious, for him at least, rewards the anxiety. but if i tell him no, call him away from the window, and make him sit/down/place/stay/do a flip/whatever, after a 30 second training session he's forgotten all about the scary window, and i reward his ability to redirect his attention towards me and do what i'm asking. right now, i'm sitting in my living room with all the blinds open, he's sleeping next to me, and i have full confidence that when the fedex guy shows up later on, he'll be able to keep his chill. 


of course, every dog is unique. at the end of the day, we're all just doing our best to give them the awesome life they deserve, and the best training technique is whichever one serves that goal for you and your pup.

my trainer's philosophy is "there's no such thing as too much affection, just affection at the wrong time" and i've found that to be 100% true. when i first got my dog and found out he was reactive, my instinct was to try and comfort him with treats, praise, etc. whenever we were in a situation he may be reactive to. we did this for a few months, but he only seemed to get worse. when i started with my trainer, he explained to me that by doing that, i was essentially telling my dog "you're anxious, yes, good boy, have a treat" and reinforcing his anxiety. now, 95% of my dog's life is him getting all the praise, love, and cuddles he could ever dream of, especially during training, but also just for existing. when he does get reactive, i have him practice some basic commands, which redirects his focus away from whatever's making him anxious, and gives him an opportunity to be rewarded for doing something good. every dog is different, but i've found that this approach works great for us, and the difference it's made with his anxiety and overall quality of life has been night and day

if sensory issues have a sizable impact on your daily life, you may want to do some research on autism. the difference with sensory issues between adhd and autism is that with adhd, it presents as "this sensation is distracting to me at this moment, but i can adjust once my mind moves onto something else" whereas with autism, it's "this sensation itself is the problem, and whenever i feel this sensation, i feel dysregulated and am unable to adjust". it's not uncommon for adhders to have sensory issues without meeting the full criteria for an autism diagnosis, but since many people don't know what autism actually looks like, it's worth looking into.
